text:
Over the past decade, the United States federal government’s record on press freedom and the treatment of civil society organisations has been marked by coercive legal tools, politicised intimidation, and a widening “national security” rationale used to chill scrutiny. The problem is not simply episodic misconduct by one administration: it is a durable institutional pattern spanning the presidency, the Justice Department, the national security apparatus, and Congress.

A central harm has been the federal government’s continued willingness to treat routine journalistic activity as a security threat. The Trump administration’s seizure of reporters’ phone and email records, including those of CNN, The New York Times, and The Washington Post, exemplified this pattern. Even where nominally authorised through legal process, such surveillance undermines source confidentiality, the core mechanism by which accountability reporting occurs. If sources reasonably fear exposure, they stop talking; corruption and abuse become harder to uncover. Accountability here lies first with the Department of Justice officials who sought the records, but also with attorneys general and presidents who tolerated an expansive view of leak investigations over press protections.

The Biden administration partially retreated by revising DOJ policy, but it did not fundamentally dismantle the state’s leak-investigation machinery. The continued prosecution of Julian Assange under the Espionage Act remained especially damaging because it advanced a theory under which obtaining and publishing classified information can be treated as criminal conduct rather than protected newsgathering. Whatever one thinks of Assange personally, the precedent is corrosive: it collapses the distinction between source and publisher and gives future administrations a ready-made tool against investigative media. Responsibility extends beyond DOJ to Congress, which has left the Espionage Act unreformed despite its obvious incompatibility with modern press freedom norms.

A second pattern is the weaponisation of federal power to stigmatise and burden civil society organisations, especially those engaged in protest, migrant support, or politically disfavoured advocacy. During the 2020 racial justice protests, federal law enforcement responses—particularly by the Department of Homeland Security and other federal officers deployed in Washington and Portland—relied on aggressive crowd control, broad intelligence collection, and rhetoric framing protest as a security problem. This harms civil society by raising the cost of association and participation: when activists expect surveillance, arrest, or physical force, organisations struggle to recruit, retain members, and operate openly. Accountability belongs to executive branch leadership that authorised these tactics, but also to agency cultures that routinely treat dissent through a policing lens.

The federal government has also facilitated a hostile operating environment for humanitarian and advocacy groups working on immigration. Investigations and prosecutions of border activists and aid volunteers, even when not always resulting in conviction, functioned as punitive process. The mechanism of harm is deterrence through attrition: legal defence costs, reputational damage, and uncertainty drain organisational capacity and warn others away from similar work. Here again, prosecutors and enforcement agencies bear direct responsibility, while senior political officials are accountable for constructing migration as an emergency justifying exceptional enforcement.

Another persistent danger has been the normalisation of official disinformation and retaliatory rhetoric against the press and NGOs. Trump’s repeated branding of the media as “the enemy of the people” and threats aimed at nonprofits and watchdogs did not merely debase discourse; they signalled to agencies, supporters, and local authorities that independent scrutiny was illegitimate. Such rhetoric increases harassment risks and weakens the informal norms on which legal protections depend. Although this was most explicit under Trump, institutional actors who failed to impose consequences share blame.

Overall, the federal government’s record is defined by overclassification, punitive leak enforcement, protest policing, and the securitisation of dissent. These are not isolated excesses but interlocking methods of control that narrow the space in which journalists and civil society can safely operate.
